mobilehealth.name: Mobile health
mobilehealth.section.name: Mobile health
mobilehealth.section.title: Mobile health
mobilehealth.section.desc: Checks the iOS and Android parts of a repository (Xcode project, Podfile, Gradle files, manifests, signing, permissions, store readiness) and explains each problem in plain language. It only reads files: nothing changes until you start an agent run.
mobilehealth.section.enableDesc: The panel appears only for repositories that contain an iOS or Android project.
mobilehealth.noRepo: No iOS or Android project found
mobilehealth.noRepoDesc: This panel appears for repositories with an ios or android folder, an Xcode project or a Gradle build.
mobilehealth.readOnly: Read-only. Nothing is changed until you press Ask agent to fix and start the run.
mobilehealth.summary: {errors, plural, one {# error} other {# errors}}, {warnings, plural, one {# warning} other {# warnings}}, {notes, plural, one {# note} other {# notes}}
mobilehealth.allGood: No problems found in this project.
mobilehealth.askFailed: Could not open the New run dialog
mobilehealth.confidenceTip: A guess from package names and native code. The app cannot see every way JavaScript asks for a permission.
mobilehealth.checklistNote: Only what can be seen in the repository. Store rules change: check the current requirement. Tables behind these checks were last reviewed on {compat} (build tools) and {store} (store levels).
mobilehealth.skipped.tooLarge: {file} is too large to read and was skipped.
mobilehealth.skipped.notRegular: {file} is not a plain file (a link or a special file) and was not opened.
mobilehealth.skipped.unreadable: {file} could not be understood and was skipped.
mobilehealth.skipped.stoppedSearching: The search for projects stopped early because the repository has very many folders.
mobilehealth.skipped.stoppedEarly: The scan of this repository stopped early because it took too long (a very large or unusual repository). What is shown may be incomplete.
mobilehealth.skipped.listingTruncated: The folder {file} has so many entries that only some of them were looked at.
mobilehealth.skipped.tooManyProjects: Only the first projects of this repository are shown.
mobilehealth.f.ios.team.empty.title: No Apple developer team is set for {target}
mobilehealth.f.ios.team.empty.why: Xcode needs to know which Apple developer account signs the app. Without a team, builds for a real iPhone and for the App Store fail with a signing error.
mobilehealth.f.ios.signing.manualNoProfi: {target} signs manually but names no provisioning profile
Manual signing needs a provisioning profile, the file from Apple that says this app may run on certain devices. Without it the build stops.
mobilehealth.f.ios.signing.automaticWith: {target} uses automatic signing but also names a profile
With automatic signing Xcode picks the profile itself, so the named one is ignored or causes a clash. It is confusing at best.
mobilehealth.f.ios.bundleId.missing.why: The bundle identifier is the app's unique name on Apple's systems. Without it the app cannot be signed or uploaded.
The bundle identifier {bundleId} looks like a template placeholder
It came with the project template. Your app needs its own identifier, registered in your Apple developer account, and it is hard to change after release.
mobilehealth.f.ios.bundleId.configsDiffe: {target} uses different bundle identifiers in its configurations
Debug and Release have different identifiers ({values}). That is fine for a separate test app and a mistake otherwise: push notifications and sign-in then work in one build and not in the other.
mobilehealth.f.ios.bundleId.extensionPre: Extension {target} has an identifier that does not start with the app's
An extension's identifier ({bundleId}) must be the app's identifier ({appBundleId}) followed by a dot and a name. Otherwise the App Store rejects the upload.
mobilehealth.f.ios.version.marketingDiff: The iOS version is not the same everywhere in the project
The app and its extensions use different version numbers ({values}). The App Store expects one version for the whole app.
mobilehealth.f.ios.version.buildDiffer.t: The iOS build number is not the same everywhere
mobilehealth.f.ios.version.buildDiffer.w: The app and its extensions have different build numbers ({values}). Uploads can be refused or confuse TestFlight.
mobilehealth.f.ios.version.plistOverride: Info.plist overrides the version set in Xcode
Info.plist spells out version {plistVersion}, while the Xcode setting says {projectVersion}. The spelled-out one wins, so changing the Xcode setting changes nothing.
mobilehealth.f.ios.deployment.inconsiste: {target} has different minimum iOS versions in its configurations
The oldest iOS version the app supports is not the same in every configuration ({values}), so Debug and Release builds can behave differently.
mobilehealth.f.ios.deployment.mismatch.t: Podfile says iOS {podfile}, the Xcode project says iOS {project}
mobilehealth.f.ios.deployment.mismatch.w: The libraries and the app disagree about the oldest iPhone software they support. If the libraries ask for a newer one the build fails; the other way round it only warns.
mobilehealth.f.ios.entitlements.fileMiss: The entitlements file {entitlements} does not exist
The project points to an entitlements file (the list of special abilities such as push notifications) that is not there, so the build fails.
mobilehealth.f.ios.permission.missing.wh: The app seems to use it (basis: {basis}), but Info.plist has no text explaining why. iOS closes the app the moment it asks, and App Store review rejects it. This is a guess: check that the app really uses it.
The permission text shown to users is blank. Apple rejects apps with an empty text, and users see nothing useful when asked.
mobilehealth.f.ios.push.entitlementMissi: Push notifications look used, but the entitlement is missing
The app seems to use push notifications (basis: {basis}), but no entitlements file contains the push setting. On a real iPhone, signing up for notifications fails.
mobilehealth.f.ios.pods.lockMissing.why: This file pins the exact versions of the iOS libraries. Without it each install may pick different versions, and builds stop being repeatable.
mobilehealth.f.ios.pods.notInstalled.tit: The iOS libraries (Pods) are not installed
mobilehealth.f.ios.pods.notInstalled.why: Xcode cannot build until pod install has been run. This is normal in a fresh copy of the project.
mobilehealth.f.ios.pods.outOfSync.title: The installed iOS libraries do not match Podfile.lock
mobilehealth.f.ios.pods.outOfSync.why: Xcode stops with the error: The sandbox is not in sync with the Podfile.lock. Running pod install again fixes it.
mobilehealth.f.ios.xcodeEnv.missing.why: React Native's Xcode build step uses this file to find Node. Without it a build started from Xcode can fail with: node: command not found.
mobilehealth.f.ios.xcodeEnv.hardcodedNod: The Node path is a folder in someone's home directory. On any other computer, or on a build server, the build cannot find Node.
mobilehealth.f.android.androidx.off.why: React Native's libraries need it. Without it the build fails with duplicate class or manifest merge errors.
mobilehealth.f.android.appId.invalid.tit: {applicationId} is not a valid Android app ID
mobilehealth.f.android.appId.invalid.why: An app ID needs at least two parts separated by dots (like com.company.app), each starting with a letter. The Play Store refuses anything else.
mobilehealth.f.android.appId.placeholder: The app ID {applicationId} looks like a template placeholder
Once the app is on the Play Store its ID can never change. Choose the real one before the first upload.
The wrapper downloads the exact Gradle version the project was written for. Without it every computer needs the right Gradle installed by hand.
mobilehealth.f.android.gradle.tooOld.tit: Gradle {gradle} is too old for Android Gradle plugin {agp}
mobilehealth.f.android.gradle.tooOld.why: This plugin version needs Gradle {min} or newer, so the build stops before it starts. The table behind this check shows its review date below.
mobilehealth.f.android.gradle.unknownAgp: Plugin {agp} is not in the compatibility table
This app's table was last reviewed on {reviewed}, so it cannot tell whether Gradle {gradle} is enough for it. Look it up on developer.android.com.
mobilehealth.f.android.keystore.notIgnor: Signing key {file} is not hidden from git
Anyone who gets the repository could sign apps as you. Key files must stay out of git.
mobilehealth.f.android.manifest.cleartex: The app allows unencrypted web traffic
Plain http connections can be read and changed by anyone on the network. It is usually only needed while developing against a local server.
mobilehealth.f.android.manifest.debuggab: Anyone can attach a debugger and read the app's data. The Play Store rejects apps like this.
mobilehealth.f.android.namespace.missing: The Android module has no namespace
Newer Android build tools refuse to build without it. It is the package name used inside the code.
mobilehealth.f.android.permission.sensit: {name} is a permission the Play Store reviews closely
Apps that ask for it usually have to fill in a declaration form and explain why. Check the current policy, and remove it if nothing needs it.
mobilehealth.f.android.permission.undecl: The app seems to use it (basis: {basis}), but the manifest does not list the permission. The feature then fails on Android, unless a library adds it for you.
mobilehealth.f.android.permission.unused: {name} is declared but nothing seems to use it
Every permission is shown to people in the store. Extra ones cost trust and can trigger extra review. This is only a guess, so check before removing.
mobilehealth.f.android.sdk.compileMissin: Gradle needs to know which Android version to compile against. Without it the build stops.
mobilehealth.f.android.sdk.targetAboveCo: The app cannot target an Android version it is not compiled against. Raise compileSdk or lower targetSdk.
mobilehealth.f.android.sdk.minAboveTarge: The oldest supported Android cannot be newer than the one the app is built for. Android Studio treats it as an error.
mobilehealth.f.android.sdk.targetMissing: Without it the app behaves as if it were built for its oldest supported Android, and the Play Store refuses uploads.
mobilehealth.f.android.sdkDir.missing.ti: Gradle may not find the Android SDK
mobilehealth.f.android.sdkDir.missing.wh: There is no sdk.dir in local.properties and no ANDROID_HOME that this app can see. Builds started from a terminal fall back to the shell's setting; Android Studio writes the file for you.
mobilehealth.f.android.secrets.plaintext: A password is written in plain text ({key})

Passwords in project files end up in git and in every copy of the project. Move it to an environment variable and change the password, since it has already been exposed. Its value is never shown here.
mobilehealth.f.android.signing.absoluteK: Signing config {config} points to a folder on one computer
The key file path starts in someone's home folder, so nobody else, and no build server, can sign.
mobilehealth.f.android.signing.keystoreM: Key file {keystore} for {config} does not exist
Building with this signing setup fails. A release key is often kept out of git on purpose, so ask where it is rather than making a new one: a new key cannot update an app that is already published.
mobilehealth.f.android.signing.releaseUs: The release build is signed with the debug key
The Play Store rejects such uploads, and an app signed that way can never be updated with the real key.
mobilehealth.f.android.version.codeInval: The Play Store only accepts whole numbers from 1 to 2,100,000,000, and every update needs a higher one.
mobilehealth.f.android.version.missing.w: Without versionCode and versionName every build is version 1, and the Play Store will not take an update.
mobilehealth.f.cross.version.mismatch.ti: iOS is on {ios}, Android is on {android}
mobilehealth.f.cross.version.mismatch.wh: They may differ on purpose when the apps ship separately. Most teams keep them equal so support and release notes stay simple.
mobilehealth.f.cross.bundleId.mismatch.w: They are allowed to differ. Using one ID makes Firebase, deep links and store pages easier to keep straight. Both are permanent once published.
mobilehealth.f.cross.newArch.mismatch.ti: New Architecture is {ios} on iOS but {android} on Android
mobilehealth.f.cross.newArch.mismatch.wh: Libraries behave differently with and without it, so bugs show up on one platform only. Pick one setting for both.
mobilehealth.f.cross.hermes.mismatch.tit: The Hermes engine is {ios} on iOS but {android} on Android
mobilehealth.f.cross.hermes.mismatch.why: Speed and some language features differ between JavaScript engines. Make sure it is intended.
mobilehealth.f.env.notIgnored.title: {file} is not hidden from git
mobilehealth.f.env.notIgnored.why: Environment files usually hold secrets such as API keys. Add them to .gitignore so they are never committed. Only the file name was looked at, never its content.
mobilehealth.f.env.missing.title: {package} reads a .env file, but there is none
mobilehealth.f.env.missing.why: In a fresh copy of the project the file is missing because it is kept out of git. Copy the example file if there is one and ask the owner for the values.
mobilehealth.f.expo.bundleId.drift.title: app.json and the native project disagree on an identifier
mobilehealth.f.expo.bundleId.drift.why: app.json says {expo} for {key}, the native project says {native}. Whichever is regenerated later wins, which can silently change the app's ID.
mobilehealth.f.expo.version.drift.title: app.json and the native project disagree on a version
mobilehealth.f.expo.version.drift.why: app.json says {expo} for {key}, the native project says {native}. The native files are what gets built; app.json only matters if they are regenerated.
mobilehealth.f.expo.config.dynamic.title: app.config is a script and was not read
mobilehealth.f.expo.config.dynamic.why: It is code, so it is never run here, for safety. Its version and IDs could not be compared with the native projects.

mobilehealth.c.ios.privacyManifest.missi: Not found. Apple's rules for these files change, so check the current requirement.

mobilehealth.c.android.targetApi.ok: targetSdk {target} reaches level {level}, the one noted in this app's table (reviewed {reviewed}). Check the current requirement on Google Play.
mobilehealth.c.android.targetApi.missing: targetSdk {target} is below level {level}, the one noted in this app's table (reviewed {reviewed}). Check the current requirement on Google Play.
mobilehealth.c.android.targetApi.check: targetSdk could not be read. This app's table notes level {level} (reviewed {reviewed}): check the current requirement on Google Play.
mobilehealth.c.android.screenshots.title: Store screenshots
mobilehealth.c.android.screenshots.check: Not found in the repository. They may be kept elsewhere: check the Play Console.
